report:
**Conclusion:** The claim that *increasing the number of childhood vaccines causes autism* is not supported by reliable scientific evidence.

**Why the claim is raised:** Some proponents cite correlations between rising autism diagnoses and expanding vaccine schedules, or small “vaccinated versus unvaccinated” studies. Correlations cannot establish causation: autism identification, diagnostic definitions, services, and awareness have also changed substantially. Such comparisons are especially vulnerable to selection bias, incomplete records, and confounding (for example, healthcare use affects both vaccination documentation and likelihood of receiving an autism diagnosis).

**Direct evidence on “more” exposure:** A case-control study calculated each child’s cumulative exposure to vaccine antigens through ages 3 months, 7 months, and 2 years using immunization registries and medical records. It found no association with autism spectrum disorder—directly testing the “too many, too soon” hypothesis.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23545349/

A meta-analysis combining five cohort studies (1,256,407 children) and five case-control studies (9,920 children) likewise found vaccination was not associated with autism/ASD.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24814559/

More recently, a nationwide Danish registry cohort of over 1.2 million children examined variation in cumulative aluminum exposure from childhood vaccines—one proposed mechanism—and found no association with neurodevelopmental conditions including autism.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40658954/

The National Academies’ independent review concluded that epidemiologic evidence favored rejecting a causal relationship between MMR or thimerosal-containing vaccines and autism.  
https://www.nationalacademies.org/publications/10997

No observational study can prove risk is literally zero, and research continues on autism’s causes. But the best, large-scale evidence does not show that a higher number of childhood vaccines—or higher antigen/adjuvant exposure—causes autism.
